# When Things Fail {#chp:errors}

Errors are normal, especially with networks and files. What matters is how
little code you need to handle them. This chapter has three short recipes.

## Ask whether code throws an error {#sec:try-error}

You do not always need the error, only whether there was one. `try_error()`
returns `TRUE` or `FALSE` and does not stop the script, which is less clunky
than a `tryCatch()`:

```{r}
try_error(log(1))
try_error(log("a"))
```

## Try quietly {#sec:try-silent}

`try_silent()` behaves like `try(silent = TRUE)`: it does not print the error
message, and returns an object of class `try-error` if something went wrong:

```{r}
z = try_silent(sqrt("x"))
inherits(z, "try-error")
```

## Retry a flaky operation {#sec:retry}

Network calls fail for no good reason. `retry()` calls a function repeatedly
until it succeeds or the attempts run out, pausing between tries:

```r
# retry a download up to 3 times, waiting 5 seconds between attempts
retry(download.file, url = "https://example.com/data.csv", destfile = "data.csv")
```


## Run cleanup when the caller exits {#sec:exit-call}

`on.exit()` only works for the function it is written in. `exit_call()` lets a
helper register cleanup in its *parent* function, as if the parent had called
`on.exit()` itself. Here `setup()` registers the message, and it fires when
`task()` finishes:

```{r}
setup = function() {
  cat("setting up\n")
  exit_call(function() cat("cleaning up\n"))
}
task = function() {
  setup()
  cat("working\n")
}
task()
```

Use `n = 3` to target the grandparent, and so on.
